newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Aborigines see PM as obstacle to racial harmony.
newsitem.headline: Aborigines see PM as obstacle to racial harmony.

text.p: Aborigines say one person may stand in the way of Australia's efforts to mend racial divisions -- and they are not talking about race row politician Pauline Hanson.
For once, the leader of Australia's fledgling far-right One Nation party is no longer cast as the only real villain in the bitter race debate engulfing Australia.
That part now also belongs to Prime Minister John Howard, if angry comments expressed at this week's historic Aboriginal Reconcilation Convention are any guide.
Aboriginal leader Noel Pearson summed up the prevailing mood of the three-day conference when he said Australia's political leaders did not have their heart in Aboriginal reconciliation.
"There is a pressing need for a moral or philosophical lobotomy or heart transplant on the part of our national leadership," Pearson told the conference to loud applause.
In a week which saw the opposition leader weep in parliament over the past treatment of Aborigines, there was little doubt Pearson's comment was aimed primarily at the prime minister.

A scion of Australia's white, conservative middle class, Howard has upset Aborigines with decisions on two main issues: the nation's 200-year-old conflict over land and a past official practice of taking Aboriginal children from their parents.

In a lectern-thumping speech to a mainly hostile audience of almost 2,000 conference delegates on Monday, Howard defended his plan to water down a recent High Court ruling which enabled Aborigines to share land with farmers.
Before the court ruling, pastoral leases, covering 40 percent of the continent's 7.68 million square km (2.96 million square miles), were thought safe from land claims by Aborigines.

Howard also announced this week his government would not pay compensation to tens of thousands of "Stolen Generation" Aborigines forcibly taken from their parents under a policy of white assimilation which survived into the 1960s.
A human rights report presented to parliament this week called the practice attempted genocide and urged compensation. The document moved Labor opposition leader Kim Beazley to tears.
But a dry-eyed Howard said Australians should not be forced to accept liability "for the acts of earlier generations".

It has been a tumultuous week in Aboriginal affairs, one in which indigenous, political, business and community leaders were to have spelt out an agenda for repairing black-white relations by the centenary of nationhood in 2001.
Instead, the past few days have continued a 14-month slide in Aboriginal relations since Howard's conservatives won office.
Howard feels the previous Labor government's policy on Aborigines -- which sought to not only redress past wrongs but to atone for them as well -- is to blame for the divisions.
He says former prime minister Paul Keating attempted to blacken Australia's proud history, alienating white Australia and sowing the seeds for Hanson's right-wing backlash.
Rejecting what he calls Keating's "black arm-band" view of history, Howard says his idea of reconciliation is about lifting Aborigines' appalling living standards, not empty gestures.
In a symbol of his practical approach to Aborigines' plight, he has ordered troops to bring potable water and health services to the most disadvantaged black communities in the outback.
In the meantime, his government has slashed overall funding for Aboriginal projects, cracked down on Aboriginal misuse of funds and redirected money toward his pragmatic reform agenda.

As well, Howard will not commit his government to a formal apology to the "Stolen Generation", though he has personally said he is sorry. An opinion poll has shown 65 percent of Australian wants the government to issue a formal apology.
These moves have won him few friends among Aborigines, but they do earn quiet applause from Hanson's growing band of supporters -- nine percent of the voting public at last count.
Aborigines now account for just two percent of Australia's population of 18 million and none hold a seat in parliament.
As Australia heads into the next century, possibly as a republic, Aborigines doubt if Howard, an avowed monarchist whose passion is cricket, can ensure they are not left behind.
"I think it's a difficult challenge for him...," said Pat Dodson, chairman of the Council for Aboriginal Recoinciliation.
